Name: lab.poolmanjim.com
Description:
This is the layout for a Tiered Administrative Model example including Builtin OUs.

# Domain (Example.com)
This node represents the domain root.

## Security
- Use mostly the default permissions.
- Avoid delegating full control, reset passwords, and other privileged attribute administration at this level.
- Default Domain Policy should be linked here, unchanged.
- Domain-wide user and computer policies should link here.

# Design Notes
Tiering is broken into a three-tier model assigned as follows.
- Tier 0: Identity/environment-wide administrative rights, or administrative rights to systems with control over any Tier 0 system.
- Tier 1: Business service and infrastructure administrative rights. These systems encompass most servers and, at times, even workstations. Systems whose compromise could introduce business impact or result in significant data exposure.
- Tier 2: Endpoint administration rights. These are systems users log into directly to check email and browse the web.

Each OU name should be unique. The limit on OU name length is generous, so this shouldn't be a problem. Avoid special characters other than spaces, dashes, and underscores.

Do not create OU structures more than 5 layers deep. Microsoft recommends no less than 10, so 5 leaves a healthy amount of breathing room for exceptions.

Group nesting follows the AGDLP model:
- Accounts are added to Global Groups.
- Global Groups are added to Domain Local groups.
- Domain Local groups are granted permissions on resources.

Two group types appear frequently in this design:
- Role Groups: define user, system, or functional roles.
- Resource Groups: map 1:1 to a permission on a resource type.

Children.Name: Admin
Children.Description:
This OU is the parent OU for privileged objects.

## Security
- Disable ACL inheritance.
- Grant only Domain Admins/T0 Admins modify/change permissions and the ability to create new OUs.
- Zero/Limited Group Policies.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

## Immediate Children
- Only other OUs/Containers.

Children.Name: Tier 0
Children.Description:
This OU contains all objects and resources considered Tier 0 systems or accounts. The one exception is Domain Controllers, which always live exclusively in the Domain Controllers OU.

## What is Tier 0?
Tier 0 is defined as "control" access over the entire domain/directory and identity.

Traditionally these are accounts with Domain Admin level access. In this model these are accounts with domain-level access or the ability to influence domain controllers, domain admins, etc. Consider all access pathways here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU.
- Zero/Limited Group Policies.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T0 PAWs
Children.Description:
# T0 PAWs OU
Privileged Access Workstations for Tier 0 administrators. A PAW is a hardened, dedicated workstation used exclusively for sensitive administrative tasks. These systems should be treated as Tier 0. Any compromise of a PAW is effectively a compromise of the tier it services.

## What Goes Here
Computer accounts for the physical or virtual PAW systems assigned to Tier 0 administrators.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Apply PAW-specific GPO hardening: Credential Guard enabled, AppLocker or WDAC configured to allow only approved software, internet access blocked or heavily restricted.
- Only Domain Admins and PAW management systems should have permissions here.
- Local Administrators should be limited to specific accounts that should be elevated and/or LAPS used.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.
- Changes to the OU or its sub-objects should be strictly monitored and alerted.
- Apply hardened MS Security Baselines, CIS Benchmarks, or DISA STIGs as a configuration foundation.

## Notes
PAWs are a critical component to a complete Tier 0 security model. However, they involve a lot of work to develop and deploy. At a minimum, deploy hardened jump hosts as a starting point. They address destination security while you build toward a full PAW model that also secures the origin.

Children.Name: T0 Servers
Children.Description:
# T0 Servers OU
Servers classified as Tier 0: systems that have direct control over the domain or identity plane, or whose compromise could enable control of the domain.

## Examples
- Entra Connect / AAD Connect servers
- Active Directory Certificate Services (PKI/CA) servers
- ADFS / Federation servers
- Privileged Access Management (PAM) solutions
- Backup systems with domain-level access or access to DC backups

> NOTE: Domain Controllers belong in the Domain Controllers OU, not here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions here.
- Apply Tier 0 server hardening baselines: MS Security Baseline, CIS Benchmarks, or DISA STIGs.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T0 Service Accounts
Children.Description:
# T0 Service Accounts OU
Service accounts used by Tier 0 systems and processes. Any account here should be treated with the same sensitivity as a Domain Admin account: the services they support operate at the identity plane.

## Account Standards
- Prefer gMSAs or dMSAs (Windows Server 2025+) wherever the application supports them.
- Standalone MSAs as a fallback over traditional user accounts.
- Traditional service accounts only when no managed alternative exists, with long random passwords rotated on a defined schedule.
- No interactive logon rights.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions here.
- Apply a policy restricting interactive logon for service accounts.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T0 Users
Children.Description:
# T0 Users OU
Dedicated administrative user accounts for Tier 0 personnel. These are not day-to-day accounts. They exist solely for Tier 0 administrative tasks and should never be used for email, web browsing, or any non-administrative purpose.

## Account Standards
- Separate account from the user's standard and Tier 1/2 accounts.
- No email, browsing, or non-administrative use.
- Protected Users group membership where possible.
- MFA enforced. On-prem MFA is a challenge sometimes so you'll need to consider the options.
- Use a Fine Grained Password Policy (FGPP) to enforce a stricter password policy: 180-day max age, 21-character minimum, complexity enforced. Account lockout should be set to 15 invalid attempts, 15-minute observation window, and 15-minute lockout duration.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions here.
- T0 Users should be blocked from logging into non-Tier 0 systems.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T0 Groups
Children.Description:
# Tier 0 Groups OU
This OU contains all groups used to grant permissions or define roles on Tier 0 systems.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T0 Resource Groups
Children.Description:
# T0 Resource Groups OU
This OU contains all resource groups used to specifically grant permissions to T0 resources. This can be any kind of resource: file shares, AD objects, and systems themselves.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T0 Role Groups
Children.Description:
# T0 Role Groups OU
This OU contains all role groups used to define either categorization roles ("Systems Engineer", "Identity Administrator") or functional roles ("Domain Admin Delegate", "PKI Administrator") for computers or users in the Tier 0 space.

These groups are added as members of the specific resource groups that correspond to their required access.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: Tier 1
Children.Description:
# Tier 1 OU
This OU contains all objects and resources considered Tier 1 systems or accounts.

## What is Tier 1?
Tier 1 is defined as "server" or "service" administration rights: infrastructure administration. These are the systems responsible for large portions of the business technology stack that aren't Tier 0.

Traditionally this was limited to "servers" but a server is just a computer that runs a service. Tier 1 is best understood as a functional security boundary, not a hardware category.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Mostly Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU.
- Other groups may be granted rights but should be hardened extensively (near-Tier 0 standards).
- Zero/Limited Group Policies.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Computers
Children.Description:
# T1 Computers OU
Computer accounts for Tier 1 systems: servers and infrastructure systems within the Tier 1 classification. These are systems hosting business services whose compromise could result in significant business impact or data exposure.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Domain Admins and designated Tier 1 management groups should control permissions here.
- Apply Tier 1 computer hardening baselines via Group Policy.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Servers
Children.Description:
# T1 Servers OU
Dedicated server computer accounts for Tier 1 infrastructure. Use this OU for servers that require their own management GPO scope, separate from general Tier 1 computer objects.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Domain Admins and designated Tier 1 management groups should control permissions here.
- Apply Tier 1 server hardening baselines via Group Policy.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Service Accounts
Children.Description:
# T1 Service Accounts OU
Service accounts for Tier 1 systems and services. These accounts should be scoped to the specific service they support and should never be used interactively.

## Account Standards
- Prefer gMSAs or dMSAs (Windows Server 2025+) wherever supported.
- Standalone MSAs as a fallback.
- Traditional accounts only when necessary, with strong passwords and no interactive logon rights.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins and designated Tier 1 admins should have permissions here.
- Apply a policy restricting interactive logon for service accounts.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Users
Children.Description:
# T1 Admin Users OU
Dedicated administrative user accounts for personnel who administer Tier 1 systems. These are separate from the user's standard day-to-day account and should never be used for email, web browsing, or non-administrative tasks.

## Account Standards
- Separate from standard and Tier 2 accounts.
- MFA enforced.
- Protected Users group membership recommended.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins and Tier 1 admins should have permissions here.
- Apply policy restricting logon to Tier 1 systems only.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Groups
Children.Description:
# Tier 1 Groups OU
This OU contains all groups used to grant permissions or define roles on and for Tier 1 systems and users.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Resource Groups
Children.Description:
# T1 Resource Groups OU
This OU contains all resource groups used to specifically grant permissions to T1 resources. This can be any kind of resource: file shares, within AD, and to systems themselves.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T1 Role Groups
Children.Description:
# T1 Role Groups OU
This OU contains all role groups used to define either categorization roles ("Systems Engineer", "Sales Servers") or functional roles ("SQL Administrator", "QuickBooks Administrator") for computers or users in the Tier 1 space.

These groups are added as members of the specific resource groups corresponding to their required access.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: Tier 2
Children.Description:
# Tier 2 OU
This OU contains all objects and resources considered Tier 2 systems or accounts.

## What is Tier 2?
Tier 2 is defined as "endpoint" administration. Unlike Tier 1, this tier does not directly contain business services: it encompasses endpoints that require management.

Tier 2 may also contain lower-criticality servers depending on the access need.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Mostly Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU.
- Other groups may be granted rights but should be hardened extensively and be at a minimum Tier 1 (ideally Tier 0).
- Zero/Limited Group Policies.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Computers
Children.Description:
# T2 Computers OU
Computer accounts for Tier 2 endpoint systems: workstations, laptops, and other end-user devices. This is typically the largest OU in the Admin tier by object count.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Domain Admins and designated Tier 2 (endpoint) management groups should control permissions here.
- Apply endpoint hardening baselines via Group Policy.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Servers
Children.Description:
# T2 Servers OU
Servers classified as Tier 2: systems that do not host business-critical services but still require domain membership and management. Examples include low-criticality utility servers or systems that primarily support the endpoint environment.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Domain Admins and designated Tier 2 management groups should control permissions here.
- Apply appropriate server hardening baselines via Group Policy.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Service Accounts
Children.Description:
# T2 Service Accounts OU
Service accounts for Tier 2 systems and processes. Lowest privilege tier for service accounts: follow least-privilege principles and prefer managed accounts.

## Account Standards
- Prefer gMSAs or dMSAs (Windows Server 2025+) wherever supported.
- Traditional accounts require strong passwords and no interactive logon rights.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only appropriate admin groups should have permissions here.
- Apply a policy restricting interactive logon for service accounts.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Users
Children.Description:
# T2 Admin Users OU
Dedicated administrative user accounts for personnel who manage endpoint systems. Separate from the user's standard day-to-day account and scoped to endpoint administration only.

## Account Standards
- No server or identity administration from these accounts.
- MFA enforced.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins and designated endpoint admins should have permissions here.
- Apply policy restricting logon to Tier 2 systems only.
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Groups
Children.Description:
# Tier 2 Groups OU
This OU contains all groups used to grant permissions or define roles on and for Tier 2 systems and users.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Resource Groups
Children.Description:
# T2 Resource Groups OU
This OU contains all resource groups used to specifically grant permissions to T2 resources. This can be any kind of resource: file shares, within AD, and to systems themselves.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: T2 Role Groups
Children.Description:
# T2 Role Groups OU
This OU contains all role groups used to define either categorization roles ("Helpdesk Technician", "Desktop Support") or functional roles ("Workstation Imaging", "Software Deployment") for computers or users in the Tier 2 space.

These groups are added as members of the specific resource groups corresponding to their required access.

> NOTE: You could theoretically use a container over an OU here.

## Security Settings
- Inherited from parent.
- Only Domain Admins/Enterprise Admins should have permissions to this OU and its contents.
- Zero Group Policies (no policy processing objects here).
- Configure SACLs to monitor for changes.

Children.Name: Corporate
Children.Description:
# Corporate OU
The Corporate OU contains all standard (non-privileged) user, computer, group, and service account objects: the production or business space representing the organization's day-to-day workforce and systems.

Objects here are not part of the administrative tier structure. Standard users, corporate computers, distribution lists, and similar objects belong here.

Group Policy for end-user workstation configuration, software deployment, and security baselines should be applied within this OU and its children.

Children.Name: Bind Accounts
Children.Description:
# Bind Accounts OU
Service and application accounts used for LDAP bind operations: typically directory-reader accounts used by applications to query Active Directory.

## Account Standards
- Read-only permissions scoped to only what the application requires. No write access.
- Prefer gMSAs where the application supports LDAP with managed credentials.
- One account per application. No shared bind accounts.
- Audit regularly: these accounts frequently accumulate permissions over time.

## Security Settings
- Restrict interactive logon via Group Policy.
- Monitor for unusual query patterns via SACL or SIEM.

Children.Name: Computers
Children.Description:
# Computers OU
Computer accounts for corporate endpoint systems: standard workstations and laptops used by corporate users for day-to-day work.

> NOTE: This is distinct from the T2 Computers OU in the Admin tier, which holds computer accounts under Tier 2 administrative control.

## Security Settings
- Apply endpoint hardening GPOs appropriate for corporate users.
- Software deployment, configuration management, and security baselines applied here.

Children.Name: Users
Children.Description:
# Users OU
Standard corporate user accounts, organized by geographic region. Each regional sub-OU allows for region-specific GPO application and delegated administration where needed.

## Design Notes
Geographic organization works well when GPOs or administrative delegation differs by region. If all regions are managed identically, consider flattening to a single Users OU. OU structures are not free: they add complexity to administration and troubleshooting.

Children.Name: Africa
Children.Description:
# Africa Users OU
User accounts for the Africa region. Apply Africa-specific GPOs here: logon hours, locale settings, regional proxy configuration, etc.

If no region-specific policy differences exist, reconsider whether this sub-OU adds value.

Children.Name: Asia
Children.Description:
# Asia Users OU
User accounts for the Asia region. Apply Asia-specific GPOs here: logon hours, locale settings, regional proxy configuration, etc.

If no region-specific policy differences exist, reconsider whether this sub-OU adds value.

Children.Name: EU
Children.Description:
# EU Users OU
User accounts for the EU region. Apply EU-specific GPOs here: logon hours, locale settings, GDPR-relevant configuration, regional proxy settings, etc.

If no region-specific policy differences exist, reconsider whether this sub-OU adds value.

Children.Name: US
Children.Description:
# US Users OU
User accounts for the US region. Apply US-specific GPOs here: logon hours, locale settings, regional proxy configuration, etc.

If no region-specific policy differences exist, reconsider whether this sub-OU adds value.

Children.Name: Distribution Lists
Children.Description:
# Distribution Lists OU
Mail-enabled groups used for email distribution: typically Exchange or Microsoft 365 distribution lists.

## Notes
- These are not security groups. Do not use them for resource access.
- Membership is typically managed by email administrators or via self-service through Exchange/M365 admin portals.
- Review membership periodically. Stale distribution lists accumulate over time and create confusion.

Children.Name: Domain Controllers
Children.Description: Default OU for domain controller computer accounts

Children.Name: Builtin
Children.Description:
# Builtin Container
Default Windows AD container for built-in security principals. Created automatically during domain creation and cannot be deleted or moved. This is a Tier 0 container and should be secured accordingly.

Contains built-in groups including Administrators, Backup Operators, Account Operators, and others. Membership in these groups carries significant privilege. Review and restrict membership as appropriate.

## Security Settings
- Harden ACLs on this container: only Domain Admins and Enterprise Admins should have modify permissions.
- Remove any delegated permissions that should not be here.
- Configure SACLs to audit all changes to the container and group memberships within it.
- Note: as a Container (not an OU), Group Policy cannot be linked here directly. Hardening is enforced through ACL controls and monitoring.

## Notes
- This container should not be used for anything other than its default objects.
- Monitor membership changes in all groups here via SACLs and your SIEM.

Children.Name: Computers
Children.Description:
# Computers Container
Default container for computer accounts that join the domain without a specified target OU. In a well-managed environment this container should be nearly empty.

Monitor this container. Rogue or unmanaged systems accumulate here.

## Best Practice
Use `redircmp` to redirect new computer joins to a staging OU within your managed structure. From there, systems can be reviewed, named, and moved to their target OU before going into production.

Children.Name: ForeignSecurityPrincipals
Children.Description:
# ForeignSecurityPrincipals Container
Contains security principal objects representing users and groups from external trusted domains. Populated automatically by Active Directory when external principals are added to domain local groups.

Do not manually manage objects here. Creation and deletion is handled by AD as trust relationships are established and modified.

Children.Name: Keys
Children.Description:
# Keys Container
Stores key credential objects used by Windows Hello for Business. Populated automatically by the Key Distribution Service (KDS).

Do not manually manage objects here. This container is managed entirely by Active Directory and Windows Hello infrastructure.

Children.Name: Managed Service Accounts
Children.Description:
# Managed Service Accounts Container
Default container for Managed Service Account objects. Created automatically during domain preparation. This is the default landing location for all MSA-type accounts unless a different path is specified at creation.

This container should not be used. Instead, create MSA objects in the appropriately tiered Service Accounts OU.

Monitor this container. Accounts created here bypass the tiered OU structure.

Children.Name: Users
Children.Description:
# Users Container
Default container for user and group accounts. Contains several built-in accounts and the default domain security groups.

## Key Objects
- **Administrator**: Built-in domain administrator. Rename this account and restrict its use to break-glass scenarios only. Additionally, this account can be moved to one of the secured OUs.
- **Guest**: Ensure this account is disabled.
- **krbtgt**: The Kerberos service account. Never modify this account directly. Follow Microsoft's documented procedures for krbtgt password resets. Monitor this account heavily.
- **Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins**: Highest privilege groups. Membership should be minimal, audited, and reviewed regularly. These groups may be moved to secured OUs and should be monitored appropriately.

New accounts should not be created in this container in a managed environment. Use the appropriate OU structure.

## Best Practice
Use `redirusr` to redirect new user object creation to a managed OU. New accounts created without a specified path will otherwise land here.
